design_rules: Target minimum wall thickness of 0.8–1.0 mm for 6061/6082 in small features; 1.0–1.5 mm for larger spans. Increase thickness for tall walls (height/thickness ≤ 10:1; ideally ≤ 6:1).
Use ribs, gussets, and local bosses to stiffen large panels; prefer constant wall thickness to reduce distortion and machining time.
Add generous internal fillets to pockets: radius ≥ tool radius (prefer 3 mm+); use corner reliefs (‘dog-bones’) for mating sharp-cornered parts.
Minimize unsupported wall height during machining. Sequence ops to leave material for rigidity, then finish thin areas last with light stepovers/stepdowns.
Plan tool access: avoid deep, narrow pockets (L/D ≤ 3 for end mills where possible). For deeper cavities, use larger tools, extended reach cautiously, or 5-axis to shorten stick-out.
Control chatter: use sharp tools, high helix aluminum cutters, climb milling, proper coolant. Leave 0.2–0.5 mm stock for a finishing pass to clean deflection marks.
Manage residual stress and warp: rough both sides, balance material removal, consider stress-relieved plate/bar, and optional intermediate stress relief for large/thin parts.
Design for fixturing: include sacrificial tabs/skins, datum pads, and flat clamping areas; consider vacuum or custom soft jaws for thin panels.
Keep hole edges and threads away from thin edges; use inserts or through-nuts in walls < 2× thread pitch; provide spotfaces for perpendicular seating.
Specify realistic tolerances and flatness; separate critical datums from thin flexible features; call out cosmetic vs functional surfaces to reduce cost.

answer_json.summary: Thin-walled aluminum parts are prone to deflection, chatter, and warping. Keep walls as thick and short as function allows, add ribs, and maintain constant thickness. Provide large internal fillets and reliefs for tool access. Sequence machining to keep material for rigidity and finish thin areas last with light cuts. Limit tool stick-out and pocket depth; consider 5-axis for reach. Use sharp, high-helix aluminum tools and leave stock for a final skim. Balance material removal on both sides and use stress-relieved stock to reduce distortion. Design for fixturing with tabs, datum pads, and vacuum or soft jaws. Keep threads and seats away from thin edges or use inserts. Apply only necessary tolerances and distinguish cosmetic from functional surfaces. Clarify alloy, tolerances, size, machine/fixturing, finish, and loads to finalize the design.

design_rules: Choose climb milling (down-milling) on rigid CNC machines with low backlash and solid workholding; it improves surface finish, tool life, and dimensional accuracy.
Prefer conventional milling (up-milling) on manual machines or any setup with noticeable backlash, flexible spindles, or marginal fixturing to avoid tool pull-in.
Use climb milling for finishing passes and light radial engagement (ae ≤ 30% D) to reduce rubbing and burrs on the exit edge.
Use conventional milling for heavy scale, abrasive skin (cast/forged), or interrupted surfaces to protect the cutting edge at entry.
For slotting (ae ≈ 100% D), default to conventional or use balanced trochoidal/HSM paths; climb slotting risks grabbing if rigidity is limited.
Thin walls and delicate features: climb milling reduces pushing the wall away (lower radial force), improving accuracy; keep light stepovers and sharp tools.
Workholding with pull-prone methods (vise with limited grip, vacuum, magnets): avoid aggressive climb entries; reduce chip load or switch to conventional.
Chip evacuation: climb produces thicker-to-thinner chips that evacuate rearward; conventional sends chips forward—prefer climb with flood/air and good extraction.
Adjust feeds: climb supports higher chip loads at small ae (chip thinning); conventional often needs slightly lower fz to control rubbing and heat.
Tolerances/finish: climb on finish pass, small ae/ae, sharp cutters, stable coolant; conventional when seeking more predictable cutting force direction on flexible setups.

answer_json.summary: Default to climb milling on rigid CNCs with solid fixturing—especially for finishing and light stepovers—because it lowers cutting forces, improves surface finish, and extends tool life. Choose conventional milling on manual or flexible machines, with backlash risk, marginal workholding, or when cutting through scale/abrasive skin or fully slotting without HSM paths. For thin walls, prefer climb with small radial engagement to limit deflection. With vacuum or low-friction clamping, avoid aggressive climb entries to prevent pull-in. Climb supports higher chip loads at small stepovers due to chip thinning; conventional often needs reduced feed to control heat and rubbing. Always align the choice with material, machine rigidity, workholding, operation (rough/finish), radial/axial engagement, and tolerance/finish targets.

design_rules: Limit pocket depth-to-tool diameter: aim ≤3×D for standard carbide end mills; 3–6×D requires necked/long-reach tools and raises cost/time; >6×D generally redesign (machine from both sides, make a through feature, or split the part).

Size internal corner radii to the tool: use generous fillets (radius ≥ tool radius; preferably ≥1.5× tool radius). Add relief ‘dog-bone’ or end pockets so the cutter can turn without full-width engagement.
Maintain pocket floors thick enough for rigidity and heat: target ≥1.0–1.5 mm for shallow features; for deep pockets (>3×D), increase to ≥2.0–3.0 mm or redesign to avoid thin floors.

Avoid tall, thin ribs that deflect: keep height-to-thickness H/t ≤10 for aluminum/brass, ≤6–8 for steels/titanium. If higher is unavoidable, add temporary support, increase thickness, or taper the rib.
Use generous root fillets at rib bases (radius ≥0.5× rib thickness, larger if possible) to reduce stress and tool chatter; avoid sharp inside corners.
Sequence and leave stock: rough in step-downs with rest machining, leave 0.2–0.5 mm (per side) on thin walls/ribs, then finish with minimal radial/axial load to limit deflection.
Minimize tool stick-out; use necked tools only as needed. If access allows, machine from both sides to halve reach and improve accuracy.
Prefer open-ended slots/pockets or add access holes to improve chip evacuation and reduce full-slotting; specify slight wall relief/taper (0.5–2°) in deep cavities to prevent rubbing.
Relax tolerances and finishes in deep cavities: avoid tight flatness/thickness callouts on pocket floors and ultra-fine Ra where long-reach tools are required.
Plan fixturing and rigidity: clamp away from thin areas; consider sacrificial tabs/webs that are removed last to stabilize tall ribs during machining.

answer_json.summary: Deep pockets and tall narrow ribs are limited by tool reach and part stiffness. Keep pocket depth within ~3× tool diameter when possible; beyond this, expect higher cost and risk. Use large internal radii and reliefs, thicker floors, open access for chips, and slight wall taper. For ribs, control deflection with conservative height-to-thickness ratios (≈≤10 for aluminum, ≤6–8 for steels/titanium), generous root fillets, and staged machining that leaves finish stock. Minimize tool stick-out, consider two-sided machining, and use temporary supports or thicker sections that are removed last. Relax tolerances and finishes in hard-to-reach areas. Final choices depend on material, exact dimensions, tolerances, tool access, and fixturing.

design_rules: Default to a general note such as “Break all sharp edges 0.2–0.5 mm” instead of modeling every chamfer; this cuts programming time and avoids dozens of CAM features for small batches.
Only model chamfers that are functional (seating, assembly, safety-critical). Leave cosmetic edge breaks as a drawing note to allow flexible, faster deburring methods.
Standardize chamfers to 45° and a limited set of sizes (e.g., 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 mm). Mixed angles/sizes drive extra tools, toolpaths, and inspection time.
Avoid tiny modeled chamfers (<0.2 mm). These often require micro tools, slow feeds, and raise risk of tool breakage; use a generic edge-break callout instead.
Keep chamfer tolerances loose (e.g., ±0.2 mm) unless function demands otherwise; tight size/angle tolerances force slower finishing and more inspection, spiking unit cost in small lots.
Prefer single-pass chamfer milling where accessible; internal/obstructed edges may require small tools or extra setups/5-axis tilting, increasing cost.
Minimize the number of unique edge orientations that need separate setups; edges on multiple faces can add flips/fixtures, which dominate cost in low volumes.
For turned parts, specify chamfers compatible with standard turning tools; milling secondary chamfers on lathe parts adds setup and per-part cost.
If many non-critical edges need softening, allow bulk deburr (tumble, brush, blast) with a burr/edge-break range; manual hand-deburr time accumulates heavily per part.
Leverage existing ops: spot drills can create entry chamfers on holes; avoid separately modeled hole chamfers unless larger than the spot angle or function-critical.

answer_json.summary: On small-batch parts, adding many modeled chamfers increases cost primarily through programming time, extra toolpaths, tool changes, and inspection—often more than raw machine cycle. Use a single drawing note like “Break all sharp edges 0.2–0.5 mm” for non-critical edges and only model functional chamfers. Standardize to 45° and a few sizes with loose tolerances (≈±0.2 mm). Avoid tiny modeled chamfers (<0.2 mm) and mixed angles. Prioritize accessible edges; internal or obstructed edges may need small tools, extra setups, or 5-axis, raising cost. Where acceptable, allow bulk deburring to replace hand-deburr. For holes, leverage spot drilling for entry chamfers. The fewer unique chamfers and the looser the tolerances, the lower the per-part cost, especially in low volumes.

design_rules: Create a unique identifier (UID) schema that links design to manufacturing: include part number, design revision, lot/serial, and work order. Use both human‑readable text and a machine‑readable code (prefer 2D DataMatrix ECC200 or QR).

Specify marking in the drawing: exact location zone, maximum area, code size (module ≥0.4 mm for DPM), marking method (laser, dot‑peen, label), and permanence class. Prohibit marks on functional/critical surfaces.

Use durable direct part marking (DPM) for metals (laser-etched or dot‑peen); for soft/coated parts use high-adhesion industrial labels or tag carriers. Verify contrast/quiet zone and validate with a verifier (ISO/IEC 29158).
Establish temporary WIP IDs when permanent marks would be damaged by upstream processes; convert to the permanent UID at the defined operation and record the linkage.

Implement digital travelers: each operation has a scannable step ID; require scans at start/complete to capture operator, machine, program file ID/hash, tool list revision, timestamp, and disposition.
Link CNC traceability: store CAM post version, NC file checksum, fixture/setup ID, probing report, and gage R&R references with the run record.

Maintain material and lot control: record raw material heat/lot and certs; propagate through cutting/nesting; manage split/merge with parent‑child relationships; serialize parts where safety/field service demands it.
Control nonconformance and rework: auto‑issue rework travelers, preserve genealogy to original UID, segregate material, and log reason codes, corrective actions, and new inspections.
Select label media for survivability: coolant/solvent/heat‑resistant labels or DPM settings; use tote/kitting labels or RFID for batches; always include human‑readable fallback.
Integrate systems (PLM/ERP/MES/QMS): single source of truth for part/revision; scanner input via APIs; role‑based access, audit trails, backups, and data retention policy.

design_rules: Define a single axial datum scheme for stack-ups (e.g., shaft shoulder as primary) and reference all axial features to it with GD&T.

answer_json.summary: Example: An HVAC blower motor used a turned steel shaft with an inner bearing seated against a shoulder, a ground spacer, and a snap-ring groove setting axial position. Individually acceptable tolerances stacked: shaft shoulder-to-end +0.10/−0.00 mm, spacer thickness ±0.03 mm, snap-ring groove location ±0.05 mm, bearing width +0/−0.01 mm, and housing counterbore depth +0.05/−0.00 mm. Worst-case created 0.18–0.22 mm unintended axial interference, over-preloading the deep-groove bearings. Symptoms were high no-load current, rapid temperature rise, and bearing noise within hours. Root causes included using mixed datums for axial features, ignoring bearing corner radius (inner ring fillet clashed with a 0.2 mm shaft chamfer), and unmodeled zinc plating on the seat. Fixes: unify axial datum to the shoulder; add relief undercut; tighten shoulder location to ±0.02 mm; specify shaft k5 fit unplated; replace washers with a single lapped spacer; introduce assembled endplay check and spin-torque limits.

design_rules: Assume 16‑ga stainless thickness t ≈ 0.060 in (1.5 mm).
For annealed 304/301 SS, target minimum inside bend radius Rmin ≈ 1.0×t ≈ 0.060 in (1.5 mm) to avoid cracking.
For 316/stronger tempers, use Rmin ≈ 1.5×t ≈ 0.090 in (2.3 mm).
In air bending, the inside radius is set mainly by die opening V: use R ≈ 0.17–0.20 × V for stainless.
Typical stainless V-opening selection: V ≈ 8–10×t. This yields R ≈ 1.3–2.0×t (≈0.080–0.120 in for 16‑ga).
If you must minimize radius, use a smaller V (≈6–8×t) and a punch nose ≈ desired R, but verify press tonnage and risk of marking.
Bend with grain transverse to reduce cracking risk; if bending parallel to grain, increase R by ≥25–50%.
Use polished, larger punch radii and protective films to limit galling and surface damage on stainless.
Account for higher springback in stainless: expect 2–4° more than mild steel; adjust overbend or tooling accordingly.
Prototype: test coupons at R = 1.0×t, 1.25×t, and 1.5×t across/with grain to validate crack-free forming.
